lesson.menu_title: The Order That Came Out Wrong
lesson.menu_desc: A taverna in Athens, a plate you did not order, and what a competent speaker says instead of blaming anybody -- modal perfect for deduction -- 23 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- The Order That Came Out Wrong
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Sophia | Lesson 4 -- The Order That Came Out Wrong
lesson.grammar_point: modal perfect for deduction (must / might / can not / should + have + past participle)

listenings.text: Okay, so the worst thing that happened to me on that trip was in a restaurant, and it was entirely my own fault. I have got a nut allergy, a serious one, and I said nothing, because I was embarrassed about my English. The waiter recommended a dessert, I said yes, and it turned up covered in pistachios. Looking back, they cannot have known. I never told them. I should have said it at the door, the way you are supposed to, and the whole thing would have taken me one sentence. What I had got wrong was not the vocabulary. It was assuming that somebody would mind.

Good evening. Are you ready to order, or would you like a few more minutes? Right. The moussaka is our house dish and I would recommend it, though I should warn you it is a very large portion, so you may want to share it. If you would prefer something lighter, the grilled fish comes with salad. Now, about the pistachio dessert you asked about. I am afraid it is not available tonight. Somebody must have finished the last one before you arrived. I can bring you the yoghurt with honey instead, at the same price. And I will bring the receipt at the end, of course. Anything to drink while you decide?

reading.rtitle: Three reviews of the same taverna
paras: LEO, 14. We went twice, which tells you something. The first night our table was not ready and we ended up waiting outside for ten minutes -- they must have double-booked, because the place was packed -- and somebody brought us olives while we waited, on the house. The moussaka is one enormous portion; my dad and I shared it and still could not finish. If you are a big family, ask them to split the plates in the kitchen. They will do it, and it saves the argument.

PRIYA, 13. I have a nut allergy, a serious one, and I had been nervous about eating out in Greece for weeks. I said it at the door, before we even sat down, and the waiter wrote it on his pad -- which I should have expected, because that is what they are trained to do. Later I asked about a dessert with pistachios and he told me it was not available for me, and brought a substitute, the yoghurt with honey. Looking back, the thing I got wrong was not the Greek. It was the two years I spent assuming somebody would be annoyed.

TOM, 12. Our order came out wrong -- I had asked for the fish and the chicken turned up. I did not say anything, because my Greek is zero and my English is not much better, and I had convinced myself I might have ordered wrong myself. My sister just said, sorry, I think there has been a mix-up, and the whole thing was over in ten seconds. They cannot have heard me properly in the first place, because they apologised twice and brought the bread for free. Check the receipt at the end, though: ours still had the chicken on it.

gist.prompt: What do the three reviews have in common?
choices: All three of them had bad food and complained about it.
In each one, the person works out what probably happened instead of blaming anybody.
None of them could make themselves understood in English.

items: Leo thinks the restaurant had given their table to somebody else.
“they must have double-booked, because the place was packed” -- he is not certain, he is working it out from what he could see.
Priya says the hardest part was the language.
The opposite: “the thing I got wrong was not the Greek. It was the two years I spent assuming somebody would be annoyed.”
Tom was sure from the start that the kitchen had made the mistake.
“I might have ordered wrong myself” -- he suspected himself first, and that is exactly why he said nothing.
Tom's receipt was wrong as well as his plate.
“ours still had the chicken on it” -- the plate was fixed in ten seconds and the paper was not.

items.situation: Everyone around you has been served and your food has not arrived. Say what you think happened, without accusing anybody.
tips: Sorry -- I think our order might have been missed.
Excuse me, could you check? I think it may have gone to another table.

items.situation: The plate in front of you is not what you ordered. Fix it in one sentence.
tips: Sorry, I think there has been a mix-up. I had ordered the fish.
Excuse me -- they must have swapped ours with that table. I asked for the fish.

items.situation: You told them about your allergy at the door and the dessert still has nuts on it. Say it without blaming the waiter in front of you.
tips: I did say when we came in -- it can't have been passed on. Could I have something else?
Sorry, somebody must have missed it. I have a nut allergy, so I'll leave this one.

items.situation: You did not do the one thing you should have done, and now it is a problem. Say so.
tips: I should have said it before we ordered.
I should have checked the menu first, to be fair.

items.situation: You do not know the English word for the thing you need. Describe it instead of switching to Portuguese.
tips: It's the thing you use to pay without cash.
It's a kind of bread that's flat and you put things on top.
